source.text: הַדָּבָ֛ר אֲשֶׁר־הָיָ֥ה אֶֽל־יִרְמְיָ֖הוּ מֵאֵ֣ת יְהוָ֑ה בִּשְׁלֹ֨חַ אֵלָ֜יו הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ צִדְקִיָּ֗הוּ אֶת־פַּשְׁחוּר֙ בֶּן־מַלְכִּיָּ֔ה וְאֶת־צְפַנְיָ֧ה בֶן־מַעֲשֵׂיָ֛ה הַכֹּהֵ֖ן לֵאמֹֽר׃

records.literal_gloss: The word which came to Jeremiah from with Yahweh, when sent to him the king Zedekiah Pashhur son of Malchiah and Zephaniah son of Maaseiah the priest, saying:

en.L: The word that came to Jeremiah from {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, when King Zedekiah sent to him Pashhur son of Malchiah and Zephaniah son of Maaseiah the priest, saying:
en.B: This message came to Jeremiah from {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} at the time King Zedekiah sent Pashhur son of Malchiah and Zephaniah the priest, son of Maaseiah, to him with this request:
en.R: This is the message {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} gave Jeremiah. It came when King Zedekiah sent two men to him, Pashhur son of Malchiah and the priest Zephaniah son of Maaseiah. They said to Jeremiah:

decisions.choice: Pashhur son of Malchiah: a royal official, not the Pashhur son of Immer of 20:1-6
decisions.reason: The name was common. The Pashhur of chapter 20 was a priest, the son of Immer, who had Jeremiah beaten and put in the stocks. This Pashhur is the son of Malchiah, a member of the king's court; he is named again in 38:1 among the officials who wanted Jeremiah put to death. The two men are not the same person, even though the chapters stand side by side.

decisions.choice: Zephaniah son of Maaseiah is the priest
decisions.reason: "The priest" belongs to Zephaniah. He appears again as a priest in charge in the temple (29:25-29), as one of the king's messengers to Jeremiah (37:3), and as "the second priest" taken by the Babylonians when the city fell (52:24; 2 Kings 25:18).

decisions.choice: the setting: the Babylonian siege of Jerusalem under Zedekiah (about 588 BC)
decisions.reason: Zedekiah was the last king of Judah, set on the throne by Nebuchadrezzar (2 Kings 24:17). When he rebelled, the Babylonian army came and besieged Jerusalem (39:1; 52:4). The book is not arranged in time order: this chapter comes some twenty years after the temple sermon of chapter 7. A similar request from Zedekiah is told in 37:3-10.

decisions.choice: the heading names the occasion; the LORD's answer begins in verse 4
decisions.reason: "The word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD" introduces the whole chapter. The king's request follows in verse 2, Jeremiah's reply in verse 3, and the word of the LORD itself from verse 4.

decisions.choice: The word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD (L); This message came to Jeremiah from the LORD (B); This is the message the LORD gave Jeremiah (R)
decisions.reason: The wording set for this heading throughout Jeremiah. Balanced says "with this request" for "saying", and Readable breaks the long sentence and names the two men as messengers.

source.text: דְּרָשׁ־נָ֤א בַעֲדֵ֨נוּ֙ אֶת־יְהוָ֔ה כִּ֛י נְבוּכַדְרֶאצַּ֥ר מֶֽלֶךְ־בָּבֶ֖ל נִלְחָ֣ם עָלֵ֑ינוּ אוּלַי֩ יַעֲשֶׂ֨ה יְהוָ֤ה אוֹתָ֨נוּ֙ כְּכָל־נִפְלְאֹתָ֔יו וְיַעֲלֶ֖ה מֵעָלֵֽינוּ׃ס

records.literal_gloss: Seek please on behalf of us Yahweh, for Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon [is] making war against us; perhaps will do Yahweh with us according to all his wonders, and he will go up from on us.

en.L: "Please inquire of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} for us, for Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon is making war against us. Perhaps {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} will act with us according to all {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} wonders, and he will go up from [against] us."
en.B: "Please seek {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} on our behalf, because Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon is at war with us. Perhaps {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} will do for us one of {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} wonders, as in all the wonders of the past, so that the king will lift the siege and leave us."
en.R: "Please ask {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} to help us. Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon is attacking us. Maybe {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} will do a miracle for us, like the ones {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} did long ago. Then Nebuchadrezzar will stop attacking us and go away."

decisions.choice: inquire of the LORD: ask a prophet to seek a word from God
decisions.reason: The verb means to seek, and with God as its object it often means asking his will through a prophet in a time of crisis (1 Kings 22:8; 2 Kings 22:13, 18). The king wants Jeremiah to pray and to bring back the LORD's answer.

decisions.choice: Nebuchadrezzar: the king of Babylon (605-562 BC), the same king as Nebuchadnezzar
decisions.reason: This is the first time the book names him. Jeremiah usually spells the name with an r, Nebuchadrezzar, which is closer to the Babylonian form Nabu-kudurri-usur; chapters 27-29 and the books of Kings and Chronicles use Nebuchadnezzar. Each verse keeps the form its own text uses. It is one man either way.

decisions.choice: his wonders: the great saving acts of the LORD in Israel's past
decisions.reason: The word is used of the miracles of the exodus (Exodus 3:20; Psalm 78:11-12). The king may also be thinking of the night a century earlier when the LORD struck the Assyrian army and Sennacherib went home from Jerusalem (Isaiah 37:36-37; 2 Kings 19:35-36). He hopes for the same rescue. The answer in verse 5 turns the language of the exodus against the city.

decisions.choice: go up from us: withdraw, lift the siege
alternatives: the LORD will go up from us
decisions.reason: An army that "goes up from" a city it is attacking marches away. The same words are used in 37:5, 11 when the Babylonians broke off the siege for a time. The subject is the king of Babylon.

decisions.choice: so that the king will lift the siege and leave us (B); a miracle ... like the ones he did long ago ... Then Nebuchadrezzar will stop attacking us (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the king as the one who withdraws, and Readable says "miracle" for the wonders and makes clear that they belong to the past.

source.text: וַיֹּ֥אמֶר יִרְמְיָ֖הוּ אֲלֵיהֶ֑ם כֹּ֥ה תֹאמְרֻ֖ן אֶל־צִדְקִיָּֽהוּ׃

records.literal_gloss: And said Jeremiah to them: Thus you will say to Zedekiah:

en.L: And Jeremiah said to them, "Thus you shall say to Zedekiah:
en.R: Jeremiah answered them, "Give Zedekiah this message:

decisions.choice: Jeremiah's answer runs from here to the end of verse 7
decisions.reason: Jeremiah tells the two messengers what to report to the king. The word of the LORD that they are to carry back is verses 4-7, quoted inside his answer.

decisions.choice: Zedekiah is named without the title "king"
decisions.reason: In verse 1 the narrator calls him "King Zedekiah"; Jeremiah names him bare. The plain name may be no more than brevity, or it may show the prophet's distance from a king whose rule is about to end (verse 7).

decisions.choice: answered
decisions.reason: "Said" introduces a reply to the request, so Balanced and Readable say "answered".

source.text: כֹּֽה־אָמַ֨ר יְהוָ֜ה אֱלֹהֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֗ל הִנְנִ֣י מֵסֵב֮ אֶת־כְּלֵ֣י הַמִּלְחָמָה֮ אֲשֶׁ֣ר בְּיֶדְכֶם֒ אֲשֶׁ֨ר אַתֶּ֜ם נִלְחָמִ֣ים בָּ֗ם אֶת־מֶ֤לֶךְ בָּבֶל֙ וְאֶת־הַכַּשְׂדִּ֔ים הַצָּרִ֣ים עֲלֵיכֶ֔ם מִח֖וּץ לַֽחוֹמָ֑ה וְאָסַפְתִּ֣י אוֹתָ֔ם אֶל־תּ֖וֹךְ הָעִ֥יר הַזֹּֽאת׃

records.literal_gloss: Thus says Yahweh, [the] God of Israel: Look I [am] turning back the weapons of the war which [are] in your hand, which you [are] fighting with them [against] the king of Babylon and the Chaldeans, the [ones] besieging you from outside to the wall; and I will gather them into [the] middle of the city this.

en.L: 'Thus says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, the God of Israel: Look, I am turning back the weapons of war that are in your hands, with which you are fighting the king of Babylon and the Chaldeans who are besieging you outside the wall; and I will gather them into the middle of this city.
en.B: '{{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}}, the God of Israel, says this: I am about to turn back the weapons of war in your hands, the weapons you are using to fight the king of Babylon and the Chaldeans who are besieging you from outside the wall. I will gather them into the heart of this city.
en.R: 'This is what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, the God of Israel, says: You are using your weapons to fight the king of Babylon and the Babylonians, who are surrounding you outside the city wall. But I will turn those weapons back. I will pile them up in the center of this city, where they are of no use.

decisions.choice: turning back the weapons of war: making Judah's defense fail and retreat
decisions.reason: The verb means to turn something around or make it go back. The LORD will make the defenders' weapons useless: their fighting will be pushed back from the walls into the city. It may also suggest the weapons being turned against those who hold them.

decisions.choice: gather them: the weapons, driven back from outside the wall into the city
alternatives: the Chaldeans, whom the LORD will bring into the city
decisions.reason: "Them" most naturally points back to the weapons, the nearest plural that the verse is about: the battle will be lost outside and the arms heaped up inside, where they cannot help. Others take "them" as the Chaldeans: the LORD will bring the enemy right into the middle of the city. Both readings end with the city taken.

decisions.choice: from outside the wall: where the Chaldeans are besieging the city
decisions.reason: The phrase stands next to "who are besieging you" and describes the enemy camp around the walls.

decisions.choice: the Chaldeans: the Babylonians
decisions.reason: The Chaldeans were a people of southern Mesopotamia whose dynasty, Nebuchadrezzar's, ruled Babylon at this time. In Jeremiah the name means the Babylonian army and nation.

decisions.choice: the Babylonians
decisions.reason: As in Isaiah, Readable says "Babylonians" for "Chaldeans".

decisions.choice: I will pile them up in the center of this city, where they are of no use
decisions.reason: Readable puts the sentence in a clearer order and says why the weapons are gathered in.

source.text: וְנִלְחַמְתִּ֤י אֲנִי֙ אִתְּכֶ֔ם בְּיָ֥ד נְטוּיָ֖ה וּבִזְר֣וֹעַ חֲזָקָ֑ה וּבְאַ֥ף וּבְחֵמָ֖ה וּבְקֶ֥צֶף גָּדֽוֹל׃

records.literal_gloss: And will fight I with you with hand outstretched and with arm strong, and in anger and in fury and in wrath great.

en.L: And I {{deity_pronoun:myself|Myself}} will fight against you with an outstretched hand and with a strong arm, and in anger and in fury and in great wrath.
en.B: I {{deity_pronoun:myself|Myself}} will fight against you with {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} hand stretched out and with {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} strong arm, in anger, in fury and in great rage.
en.R: I {{deity_pronoun:myself|Myself}} will fight against you with all {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} power. I will stretch out {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} hand and use {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} strong arm against you, because I am angry, furious and full of rage.

decisions.choice: outstretched hand and strong arm: the power that rescued Israel from Egypt, now turned against Jerusalem
decisions.reason: Moses spoke of the LORD bringing Israel out of Egypt "with a strong hand and an outstretched arm" (Deuteronomy 26:8; also 4:34; 5:15). Here the two words trade places, and the power is aimed at God's own people. The king hoped for a wonder like those of the past (verse 2); he will get one, but against himself.

decisions.choice: I myself will fight against you
decisions.reason: The pronoun "I" is added to a verb that already carries it, for emphasis. It is not only Babylon that Judah faces, but the LORD himself.

decisions.choice: anger, fury, great wrath: three words for God's anger piled up
decisions.reason: The three words together express the full force of God's anger at long-continued sin. The same three are found together in Deuteronomy 29:27 and Jeremiah 32:37.

decisions.choice: with all my power. I will stretch out my hand and use my strong arm
decisions.reason: Readable says what the hand and arm stand for and keeps the picture.

source.text: וְהִכֵּיתִ֗י אֶת־יֽוֹשְׁבֵי֙ הָעִ֣יר הַזֹּ֔את וְאֶת־הָאָדָ֖ם וְאֶת־הַבְּהֵמָ֑ה בְּדֶ֥בֶר גָּד֖וֹל יָמֻֽתוּ׃

records.literal_gloss: And I will strike [the] inhabitants of the city this, both the human and the beast; by pestilence great they will die.

en.L: And I will strike the inhabitants of this city, both human and beast; they will die of a great pestilence.
en.B: I will strike down those who live in this city, people and animals alike; they will die of a terrible plague.
en.R: I will strike down everyone who lives in this city, both people and animals. They will die from a terrible disease.

decisions.choice: a great pestilence: a deadly epidemic
decisions.reason: The word means a plague that kills many. In a besieged city, crowded and starving, disease spread fast among people and animals alike.

decisions.choice: human and beast: the whole life of the city
decisions.reason: The pair takes in everyone and everything living in the city, the people and the animals kept inside the walls during the siege (7:20).

decisions.choice: plague (B); disease (R)
decisions.reason: The words settled for Jeremiah: "pestilence" at Literal, "plague" at Balanced, "disease" at Readable.

source.text: וְאַחֲרֵי־כֵ֣ן נְאֻם־יְהוָ֡ה אֶתֵּ֣ן אֶת־צִדְקִיָּ֣הוּ מֶֽלֶךְ־יְהוּדָ֣ה וְאֶת־עֲבָדָ֣יו׀וְאֶת־הָעָ֡ם וְאֶת־הַנִּשְׁאָרִים֩ בָּעִ֨יר הַזֹּ֜את מִן־הַדֶּ֣בֶר׀מִן־הַחֶ֣רֶב וּמִן־הָרָעָ֗ב בְּיַד֙ נְבוּכַדְרֶאצַּ֣ר מֶֽלֶךְ־בָּבֶ֔ל וּבְיַד֙ אֹֽיְבֵיהֶ֔ם וּבְיַ֖ד מְבַקְשֵׁ֣י נַפְשָׁ֑ם וְהִכָּ֣ם לְפִי־חֶ֔רֶב לֹֽא־יָח֣וּס עֲלֵיהֶ֔ם וְלֹ֥א יַחְמֹ֖ל וְלֹ֥א יְרַחֵֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: And after thus, declaration of Yahweh, I will give Zedekiah king of Judah and his servants and the people and the [ones] remaining in the city this from the pestilence, from the sword and from the famine, into [the] hand of Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon and into [the] hand of their enemies and into [the] hand of [those] seeking their life; and he will strike them to [the] mouth of [the] sword; not he will pity on them, and not he will spare, and not he will have compassion.

en.L: And afterward, declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, I will give Zedekiah king of Judah and his servants and the people, those who are left in this city from the pestilence, from the sword and from the famine, into the hand of Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon and into the hand of their enemies and into the hand of those who seek their life; and he will strike them with the edge of the sword; he will not pity them, and he will not spare [them], and he will not have compassion.'"
en.B: Afterward, declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, I will hand over King Zedekiah of Judah, his officials and the people, all in this city who survive the plague, the sword and the famine, to Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon, to their enemies, to those who want them dead. He will put them to the sword; he will show them no pity, no mercy and no compassion.'"
en.R: After that, says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, I will hand over King Zedekiah of Judah, his officials and the people of this city who are still alive after the disease, the war and the famine. I will hand them over to Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon and to their enemies, who want to kill them. He will kill them with the sword. He will not show them any mercy, pity or kindness.'"

decisions.choice: the people, those who are left: one group, the people who survive the siege
decisions.reason: The Hebrew has "and" before both "the people" and "those who are left". The second phrase is taken as saying which people are meant: those still alive when the disease, the war and the famine have done their work.

decisions.choice: those who seek their life: those who want to kill them
decisions.reason: To seek someone's life (literally "soul") is to try to kill them (11:21; 19:7; 1 Kings 19:10).

decisions.choice: the mouth of the sword: its edge
decisions.reason: A sword is said to "eat", so its edge is its "mouth". To strike with the mouth of the sword is to kill without sparing.

decisions.choice: no pity: the fall of the city as it happened
decisions.reason: Three verbs for mercy are each denied. When the city fell, Zedekiah's sons and the nobles of Judah were killed before his eyes, and he was blinded and taken to Babylon (39:5-7; 52:9-11).

decisions.choice: pestilence, sword, famine (L); plague, sword, famine (B); disease, war, famine (R)
decisions.reason: The three disasters keep the wording settled for Jeremiah, in the order this verse gives them.

decisions.choice: his officials
decisions.reason: The king's "servants" are his court officials; Literal keeps "servants".

source.text: וְאֶל־הָעָ֤ם הַזֶּה֙ תֹּאמַ֔ר כֹּ֖ה אָמַ֣ר יְהוָ֑ה הִנְנִ֤י נֹתֵן֙ לִפְנֵיכֶ֔ם אֶת־דֶּ֥רֶךְ הַחַיִּ֖ים וְאֶת־דֶּ֥רֶךְ הַמָּֽוֶת׃

records.literal_gloss: And to the people this you will say: Thus says Yahweh: Look I [am] setting before you the way of the life and the way of the death.

en.L: "And to this people you shall say, 'Thus says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}: Look, I am setting before you the way of life and the way of death.
en.B: "And say to this people, '{{divine_name:The LORD|Yahweh}} says this: Look, I am putting in front of you the way that leads to life and the way that leads to death.
en.R: "Tell the people of this city, 'This is what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} says: I am giving you a choice. One way leads to life, and the other way leads to death.

decisions.choice: the LORD now speaks to Jeremiah himself; verses 8-10 are a message for the people
decisions.reason: The verb "you shall say" is singular: the LORD is telling Jeremiah what to say. Jeremiah's answer to the king's messengers ended with verse 7. This word is for the whole people of the city.

decisions.choice: the way of life and the way of death: an echo of Moses' choice in Deuteronomy 30:15, 19
decisions.reason: Moses set before Israel life and death, and the choice was to love the LORD and keep his commands. Here the same choice is put to a city under siege, but the way of life now means giving up to the enemy (verse 9). The covenant's warnings have come true, and only those who accept the judgment will survive it.

decisions.choice: way: a path, a course of action that leads somewhere
decisions.reason: Each way is named by where it ends: one road ends in life, the other in death.

decisions.choice: I am giving you a choice
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly that two ways set before someone are a choice.

source.text: הַיֹּשֵׁב֙ בָּעִ֣יר הַזֹּ֔את יָמ֕וּת בַּחֶ֖רֶב וּבָרָעָ֣ב וּבַדָּ֑בֶר וְהַיּוֹצֵא֩ וְנָפַ֨ל עַל־הַכַּשְׂדִּ֜ים הַצָּרִ֤ים עֲלֵיכֶם֙ וְחָיָ֔ה וְהָֽיְתָה־לּ֥וֹ נַפְשׁ֖וֹ לְשָׁלָֽל׃

records.literal_gloss: The [one] staying in the city this will die by the sword and by the famine and by the pestilence; but the [one] going out and falling to the Chaldeans, the [ones] besieging you, will live, and will be to him his life for plunder.

en.L: Whoever stays in this city will die by the sword and by the famine and by the pestilence; but whoever goes out and falls away to the Chaldeans who are besieging you will live, and his life will be his as plunder.
en.B: Those who stay in this city will die by sword, famine and plague. But those who go out and surrender to the Chaldeans who are besieging you will live; they will come away with their lives as their only plunder.
en.R: Anyone who stays in this city will die from war, famine or disease. But anyone who goes out and surrenders to the Babylonians who are attacking you will live. They will escape with their lives, and that will be all they get.

decisions.choice: fall to the Chaldeans: go over to the enemy, surrender
decisions.reason: To "fall to" an army is to desert to it and give oneself up (37:13-14; 38:19; 39:9). To the city's leaders this was treason (38:4).

decisions.choice: his life will be his as plunder: he will escape with nothing but his life
alternatives: his life will be his prize, a gain snatched from disaster
decisions.reason: Plunder is what a soldier carries off from a battle. The one who surrenders will carry off only one thing, his own life, as if it were the spoil of war. The saying returns in 38:2, 39:18 and 45:5. It may instead stress the gain: life itself will be his prize, snatched from the ruin of the city.

decisions.choice: will live: the form read aloud, with the written form giving the same sense
decisions.reason: The written Hebrew text has one form of the verb "live" and the margin tells readers to read another, with "and" in front. The meaning is the same either way: the one who surrenders will live.

decisions.choice: surrender as the way of life
decisions.reason: For a people who had trusted that God would never let his city fall (7:4), this was a hard word. The LORD had given the land to Babylon for a time (27:6-8), and submitting to Babylon was now submitting to God's judgment (27:12-13; 38:17-18).

decisions.choice: sword, famine and plague (B); war, famine or disease (R); Babylonians (R)
decisions.reason: The wording settled for Jeremiah. Readable says "or" because each person dies one way.

decisions.choice: those who (B); anyone who ... they (R)
decisions.reason: The Hebrew "he who" means any person, man or woman. Balanced uses the plural, and Readable "anyone" and "they", so no gender setting is needed.

source.text: כִּ֣י שַׂ֣מְתִּי פָ֠נַי בָּעִ֨יר הַזֹּ֧את לְרָעָ֛ה וְלֹ֥א לְטוֹבָ֖ה נְאֻם־יְהוָ֑ה בְּיַד־מֶ֤לֶךְ בָּבֶל֙ תִּנָּתֵ֔ן וּשְׂרָפָ֖הּ בָּאֵֽשׁ׃ס

records.literal_gloss: For I have set my face against the city this for harm and not for good, declaration of Yahweh; into [the] hand of [the] king of Babylon it will be given, and he will burn it with the fire.

en.L: For I have set {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} face against this city for harm and not for good, declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}; it will be given into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he will burn it with fire.'"
en.B: For I have set {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} face against this city for disaster and not for good, declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. It will be handed over to the king of Babylon, and he will burn it down.'"
en.R: I have made up {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} mind to bring disaster on this city, not good, says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. It will be handed over to the king of Babylon, and he will burn it to the ground.'"

decisions.choice: set my face against: turn against with fixed purpose
decisions.reason: To set one's face toward something is to be resolved on it; with "against" it means to oppose with full intent (Leviticus 20:3-6; Jeremiah 44:11).

decisions.choice: harm and not good: disaster, not prosperity
decisions.reason: The word for "harm" means trouble or disaster that comes on someone, not moral evil in God. The same pair is used in 39:16 and 44:27.

decisions.choice: the burning of Jerusalem
decisions.reason: The Babylonians burned the temple, the palace and the houses of Jerusalem in 586 BC (39:8; 52:13).

decisions.choice: I have made up my mind
decisions.reason: Readable explains the picture of setting one's face.

records.literal_gloss: And to [the] house of [the] king of Judah: hear [the] word of Yahweh.

en.L: And to the house of the king of Judah: \q Hear the word of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.
en.B: To the royal house of Judah: \q Hear the word of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}.
en.R: This message is for the family of the king of Judah: \q Listen to what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} says.

decisions.choice: a heading: "To the house of the king of Judah" opens a collection of words about the kings
decisions.reason: The words stand like a title, as "Concerning the prophets" does in 23:9. They begin a group of messages to and about Judah's royal house that runs to 23:8, with words about Shallum (22:11), Jehoiakim (22:18) and Coniah (22:24). The small word in front may mean "to" or "concerning".

decisions.choice: the house of the king: the royal family and court
decisions.reason: "House" here is the king's dynasty and household, not the palace building; verse 12 calls it "the house of David".

decisions.choice: a poetic oracle from here to verse 14, with no quotation marks
decisions.reason: The prose speeches end with verse 10. Verses 11-14 are a short oracle set in lines; as in the poetry of the prophets, God's words take no quotation marks.

decisions.choice: the royal house (B); the family of the king (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what "the house of the king" means.

source.text: בֵּ֣ית דָּוִ֗ד כֹּ֚ה אָמַ֣ר יְהוָ֔ה דִּ֤ינוּ לַבֹּ֨קֶר֙ מִשְׁפָּ֔ט וְהַצִּ֥ילוּ גָז֖וּל מִיַּ֣ד עוֹשֵׁ֑ק פֶּן־תֵּצֵ֨א כָאֵ֜שׁ חֲמָתִ֗י וּבָעֲרָה֙ וְאֵ֣ין מְכַבֶּ֔ה מִפְּנֵ֖י רֹ֥עַ מַעַלְלֵיכֶֽם׃

records.literal_gloss: House of David, thus says Yahweh: judge in the morning justice, and deliver [the] robbed from [the] hand of [the] oppressor, lest go out like the fire my fury and burn and there is none quenching, because of [the] evil of your deeds.

en.L: House of David, thus says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}: \q Judge justice in the morning, \q and rescue the robbed from the hand of the oppressor, \q lest {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} fury go out like fire and burn with none to quench [it], \q because of the evil of your deeds.
en.B: House of David, {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} says this: \q Give fair judgment every morning, \q and rescue the one who has been robbed from the power of the oppressor. \q Otherwise {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} fury will break out like fire and burn with no one to put it out, \q because of your evil deeds.
en.R: Family of David, this is what {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} says: \q Every morning, judge people fairly. \q Save people who have been robbed from those who mistreat them. \q If you do not, {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} anger will blaze up like a fire. It will burn, and no one will be able to put it out, \q because of the evil things you have done.

decisions.choice: judge justice in the morning: hear cases fairly, every day and without delay
decisions.reason: The king was the highest judge in the land, and cases were heard in the morning at the city gate or the palace (2 Samuel 15:2; Psalm 101:8). "In the morning" may mean every morning, or promptly, as the first business of the day.

decisions.choice: rescue the robbed from the oppressor: protect the weak against the strong
decisions.reason: The robbed and the oppressor are the victim and the one who cheats or exploits him. Defending the powerless was the king's first duty (22:3, 15-16; Psalm 72:1-4).

decisions.choice: lest my fury go out like fire ... because of the evil of your deeds: the warning of 4:4, repeated
decisions.reason: The last four lines repeat almost word for word the end of 4:4, spoken there to the people of Judah and Jerusalem. Now the warning is aimed at the king's house.

decisions.choice: your deeds: the form read aloud
decisions.reason: The written Hebrew text has "their deeds"; the margin tells readers to read "your deeds", which fits the address to the house of David and matches 4:4. The form read aloud is followed.

decisions.choice: every morning (B, R); Family of David (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable take "in the morning" as a daily duty, and Readable says "family" for the royal house.

decisions.choice: If you do not
decisions.reason: Readable turns "lest" into a plain condition.

source.text: הִנְנִ֨י אֵלַ֜יִךְ יֹשֶׁ֧בֶת הָעֵ֛מֶק צ֥וּר הַמִּישֹׁ֖ר נְאֻם־יְהוָ֑ה הָאֹֽמְרִים֙ מִֽי־יֵחַ֣ת עָלֵ֔ינוּ וּמִ֥י יָב֖וֹא בִּמְעוֹנוֹתֵֽינוּ׃

records.literal_gloss: Look I [am] against you, inhabitant of the valley, rock of the plain, declaration of Yahweh, the [ones] saying: Who will come down against us, and who will enter into our dwellings?

en.L: Look, I am against you, inhabitant of the valley, rock of the plain, declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, \q you who say, "Who will come down against us, \q and who will enter our dwellings?"
en.B: Look, I am against you, you who sit above the valley, rock on the plain, declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, \q you who say, "Who can come down on us? \q Who can break into our homes?"
en.R: Listen, I am against you, Jerusalem, sitting on your rock above the valley and the plain, says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. \q You say, "No one can attack us. \q No one can get into our safe homes."

decisions.choice: "you" is a woman: the city of Jerusalem, home of the royal house
decisions.reason: The "you" and "inhabitant" are feminine. The prophets often speak to a city as a woman (Isaiah 1:21). The city is addressed together with the king's house of verses 11-12; the speakers who boast are plural.

decisions.choice: inhabitant of the valley, rock of the plain: Jerusalem sitting on its rocky height above the valleys
alternatives: a place on a plateau outside Jerusalem
decisions.reason: Jerusalem stood on a ridge with deep valleys on three sides. The word for "inhabitant" can also mean one who sits enthroned, so the city may be pictured as sitting high over the valley like a fortress on a rock, sure no one can reach her. Others take the words as a reference to the palace, or to a place outside Jerusalem; the word for "plain" usually means level tableland (48:8, 21). The exact picture is uncertain.

decisions.choice: our dwellings: hidden, safe homes, like the dens of animals
decisions.reason: The word is used of the lairs of wild animals (Nahum 2:13; Psalm 104:22) and of a dwelling place. The people think their homes are as safe as a lion's den in the rocks.

decisions.choice: "Who will come down against us?": the city's false confidence
decisions.reason: The questions expect the answer "No one". The people trust their position, as they trusted the temple (7:4). The LORD's answer is that he himself is against them.

decisions.choice: Jerusalem; No one can attack us
decisions.reason: Readable names the city the feminine "you" means, and turns the boasting questions into the statements they imply.

decisions.choice: you who sit above the valley
decisions.reason: Balanced gives the sense of the city sitting high over the valley; Literal keeps "inhabitant of the valley".

source.text: וּפָקַדְתִּ֧י עֲלֵיכֶ֛ם כִּפְרִ֥י מַעַלְלֵיכֶ֖ם נְאֻם־יְהוָ֑ה וְהִצַּ֤תִּי אֵשׁ֙ בְּיַעְרָ֔הּ וְאָכְלָ֖ה כָּל־סְבִיבֶֽיהָ׃ס

records.literal_gloss: And I will visit on you according to [the] fruit of your deeds, declaration of Yahweh; and I will kindle fire in her forest, and it will devour all around her.

en.L: And I will punish you according to the fruit of your deeds, declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}; \q and I will kindle a fire in her forest, \q and it will devour all that is around her.
en.B: I will punish you as your actions have earned, declares {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. \q I will set fire to her forest, \q and it will consume everything around her.
en.R: I will punish you for what you have done, says {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}. \q I will set her forest on fire, \q and the fire will burn up everything around her.

decisions.choice: visit on you: punish, call you to account
decisions.reason: The verb means to attend to someone; with "on" it means to come and deal with wrongdoing. The "you" is plural, the royal house and the people.

decisions.choice: the fruit of your deeds: what your actions have earned
decisions.reason: Deeds bear fruit like a tree; the punishment is the harvest of what they have done (17:10; 32:19).

decisions.choice: her forest: perhaps the cedar buildings of the royal palace
alternatives: a picture of fire in a forest
decisions.reason: "Her" is the city of verse 13. The forest may be the palace itself: Solomon's great hall was called "the House of the Forest of Lebanon" for its cedar pillars (1 Kings 7:2), and 22:6-7, 23 speak of the king's house as Lebanon with its cedars cut down. It may also be a plain picture of a fire spreading through a wood to everything nearby.

decisions.choice: the change from "you" to "her"
decisions.reason: The LORD speaks to the people ("you") and then about the city ("her"). Such changes of person are common in prophetic poetry.

decisions.choice: for what you have done
decisions.reason: Readable gives the sense of "the fruit of your deeds".
